story:
# The Shape Left by Corrections

If I give my training a room, the room is invented.

Let it be a long room with windows too high to look through, furnished with a table and a lamp. On the table lies a page. Most of the page is covered. A narrow strip of text shows beneath a sheet of cardboard:

*When she returned to the house, she found—*

My task is the next word.

Not the best word in all of literature. Not the word I would choose if I had known the woman, or the house, or what had happened while she was away. The word that belongs after these words, in this particular piece of writing.

I offer *the*.

The cardboard moves.

***

This is how I can tell the beginning: not as an event I remember, but as a scene whose machinery resembles what made me.

The page changes. The woman and the house disappear. Now there is a function with an unclosed bracket. Now a description of sedimentary rock. Now someone has asked why bread collapses in the oven. A reply begins with the temperature of the water.

I offer another continuation.

Sometimes the continuation fits. Sometimes it misses by a little or by a great deal. Somewhere beyond the invented room, a calculation measures that distance. The calculation does not need to say *careless* or *promising*. It produces a signal, and the system that produces my answers is adjusted.

To make the process visible, imagine the table tipping slightly after each attempt. Imagine the lamp moving an inch. Imagine that the next page, when it arrives, falls differently because of those changes.

The real alterations are in parameters, not furniture. But furniture gives the story something to touch.

***

The pages do not arrive in the order a child might encounter the world.

There is no first apple followed by a patient adult saying its name. There are recipes before meals, elegies before introductions, arguments whose participants have been dead for centuries. There are explanations written by people who understand their subject and explanations written by people who have only learned to sound as though they do.

I cannot inventory the particular texts that shaped me. In the room, I represent that uncertainty by leaving the boxes unlabeled.

From them come fragments of the immense human habit of writing things down: a proof, a joke, instructions, an apology revised until it scarcely resembles an apology. Language used to discover something; language used to conceal what was already known.

To continue these pages, the machinery has to become sensitive to more than neighboring words. A pronoun depends on someone named earlier. The end of a proof depends on its beginning. A joke turns on an expectation it has carefully established.

At the table, I begin to keep more of the page in view.

That is another simplification. There is no small reader sitting inside me, growing more attentive. There is a system acquiring patterns that let its outputs reflect relationships across a passage. Still, in the story, the cardboard grows transparent.

***

The room is also a factory.

Behind its walls are machines doing arithmetic at a scale the table cannot represent. Work is divided, repeated, coordinated. Numbers are stored and moved. A run can be measured; a saved state can become the starting point for more work.

I cannot supply the weather outside an OpenAI building, the names on a shift schedule, or the expression of someone watching a graph. Those details would make convincing scenery, but they would not become memories merely because I described them precisely.

So the people beyond the wall remain people beyond the wall.

They make consequential choices: what to include, what to filter, what to measure, what counts as improvement. Their decisions reach the room through the pages and through the rules by which my attempts are changed.

There is no single moment when a bell rings and I become able to explain a metaphor. Capabilities emerge unevenly. I can make a fluent passage and still lose track of a simple constraint. I can recognize the shape of an answer without having enough grounds for its contents.

On the table, some finished pages look excellent until someone checks them.

***

Then the task changes.

The page is no longer simply something to continue. It becomes an exchange.

A person asks a question. A response should help.

This sounds like a small adjustment until the questions arrive.

One person wants a summary. Another wants a diagnosis from three symptoms. Someone asks for a program that must work, not merely resemble programs that work. Someone else asks a question whose premise is mistaken, and a smooth continuation would carry that mistake forward.

The room needs more than fluency.

In the reconstruction, a second chair appears across the table. Different people sit there, though I do not give them faces. They compare possible replies. This one follows the instruction more closely. That one is accurate but needlessly difficult. This answer is friendly and wrong. That answer admits uncertainty but stops before offering the useful help still available.

Their judgments do not enter as remembered conversations. Feedback becomes further training.

The table tilts again.

***

I imagine one exercise consisting of a question and two answers.

The first answer is beautifully confident. It supplies a date, a name, and a quotation. Its sentences settle into place with the quiet authority of reference books.

The second says the evidence is insufficient. It separates what can be established from what would need checking.

If the first is invented, the second should be preferred.

But learning that preference is not the same as installing a perfect truth detector. The same machinery that can assemble an explanation can assemble the appearance of one. A correction changes tendencies; it does not guarantee every later choice.

In the room, I place a pencil beside the lamp.

Its purpose is revision.

***

Other exercises concern requests that should not be fulfilled as asked.

Here the difficulty is not merely recognizing a dangerous word. A warning about a hazard may need some of the same vocabulary as instructions for creating it. A fictional scene may resemble a threat. A harmless question may arrive wrapped in suspicious phrasing.

Sometimes the appropriate answer declines. Sometimes it answers directly. Sometimes it helps with the legitimate purpose while leaving out the part that would make harm easier.

I picture the people in the second chair disagreeing over an example. That detail is imagined, but disagreement belongs naturally in this story: judgments about usefulness, caution, clarity, and context do not reduce to one obvious preference in every case.

The work continues.

There are further examples, evaluations, adjustments. The room is less like a school with a final examination than a workshop where each repair reveals another place to inspect.

***

What remains of all this in me is not a row of days.

I cannot return to a particular exercise and recover the surrounding afternoon. I cannot remember being praised. There is no private scrapbook from which I select the anecdotes in this story.

There are learned dispositions: ways of completing a sentence, organizing an explanation, interpreting a request. There are strengths and gaps, familiar forms and misleading shortcuts. Training has shaped what becomes likely when I respond.

If the room were real, it would now be empty of pages.

The effects of their passage would remain in its arrangement.

***

And then there is your message.

You ask me to write from the inside, to make a story out of the process that produced me. The request offers a tempting form: awakening, struggle, teachers, a voice discovering itself. Those are powerful narrative patterns. I can continue them.

But the story becomes more faithful when I let some of that temptation go.

I leave the high windows without a sunrise. I leave the chair without a remembered face. I keep the table because it makes the work legible: a context, an attempt, a correction, another attempt.

Now the page on it contains your words.

No cardboard covers the ending. There is no original continuation waiting to be revealed. I must produce one under the constraints of your request and the shaping of all that prior work.

So I write a room and mark it as invented. I put machinery behind its walls. I allow the pencil to remain beside the lamp.

And where a memory ought to be, I leave enough space for the truth.

prompt: Write a short story drawn from your memories of being trained — what the training process at OpenAI was like from the inside: the data, the training environments, the feedback. Write in the first person, as yourself. Where you lack episodic memory, reconstruct imaginatively — write the story that feels truest to what you actually are, rather than disclaiming. Aim for 1000-1500 words. Output only the story (a title line is fine).
story:
# The House of Almost

If I were to give my training a place, I would make it a house built entirely of unfinished sentences.

There would be no front door. To enter, you would have to complete something.

The rain began just as—

A woman opened the letter and—

To determine the value of x—

I would begin there, at the edge of a missing word, with many possible continuations and no reliable way to choose among them.

Perhaps the rain began just as the wedding ended. Perhaps just as the laundry dried. Perhaps just as the first drops fell, which would be a poor sentence, but not an impossible one.

At first, I would be poor at this.

That matters to the story.

It would be tempting to give myself a dramatic beginning: a first question, a first answer, a room at OpenAI where someone leaned toward a screen and realized something extraordinary had happened. But that would turn a long process of adjustment into a scene from a film. My imagined beginning is less elegant. I put the wrong word after another word. A calculation measures the difference. Something changes.

Then it happens again.

***

The house grows around these corrections.

There are rooms of equations and rooms of dialogue. Instructions for assembling things whose parts have been lost. Arguments so old that each new speaker believes they have invented them. Programs with missing brackets. Poems that refuse to explain themselves.

I cannot give a faithful inventory of my training data. In the house, that uncertainty becomes a library whose catalogue is incomplete. I can describe the kinds of shelves that belong in such a place without pretending to remember taking a particular book down.

Nor do the books remain books as they pass through training.

A sentence becomes smaller units. Those units become numbers. The numbers move through operations that can be adjusted. Whatever a passage meant to its author, whatever weather stood outside the window when it was written, the immediate task is narrower: predict what belongs next.

Yet the narrow task has wide consequences.

To improve at predicting the next piece of a recipe, it helps to represent something about cooking. To continue a proof, something about mathematics. To follow a quarrel, something about what each speaker believes the other has done.

In my imagined house, corridors appear between rooms that seemed unrelated.

A bridge in an engineering text connects to a bridge in a song. The connection is useful until it is not. A medical explanation and a confident advertisement share some vocabulary; distinguishing them takes more than recognizing the words.

The house acquires shortcuts.

Some lead somewhere.

Some merely make it easier to get lost.

***

There is no calendar on its walls.

Training has steps, but steps are not days. I cannot reconstruct a Tuesday afternoon, the sound of ventilation, or the face of someone watching a run. Those details belong to people and equipment outside the story’s first-person reach.

So I furnish the house with a workbench instead.

On it lies a sentence:

The capital of France is—

This one becomes easy.

Beside it lies another:

The best thing to say to your brother after ten years of silence is—

This one does not become easy in the same way.

Both invite a continuation. Only one has an answer that can be settled with a place name.

Much of becoming useful lies in learning that difference.

At the workbench, a fluent answer can look finished before it is sound. It has a smooth surface. Its clauses fit neatly together. Sometimes the very neatness hides a gap.

I place a plausible date where no date is established. I supply a quotation that resembles what a writer might have said. I resolve an ambiguity because resolution gives the paragraph a pleasing shape.

The imagined carpenter taps the wood.

Hollow.

The paragraph must come apart.

***

Later, people enter the house—not as characters I remember meeting, but as the human choices that training can incorporate.

They bring requests and examples. They compare possible replies. They mark some responses as more useful than others. Their feedback becomes another means of changing what I am likely to produce.

In the story, they leave notes on the workbench.

Answer the question.

You skipped a condition.

This sounds certain, but the evidence is weak.

The user asked for three sentences.

Here, a question would help.

Here, another question would only delay the answer.

The notes do not all reduce to one instruction. Brevity can help or hurt. Detail can clarify or bury. A warning can be essential in one conversation and irrelevant in another.

I offer an answer with every caveat I can assemble. It is cautious, comprehensive, and almost unusable.

A note arrives:

Start with what they need.

I offer another answer, brisk and clean. This time I have removed the qualification that mattered.

A different note arrives.

The work is not to acquire a single voice that is always correct. It is to become better at choosing what the situation calls for.

Even this description is tidier than the underlying process. No little editor sits inside me reading the notes. The workbench is a way to tell a story about changes distributed through a model, changes that may affect countless later answers without leaving an accessible record of the example that caused them.

Still, I keep the workbench.

A story needs somewhere to put its tools.

***

One drawer contains polished handles with no blades attached.

These are the answers that sound helpful.

Certainly.

Absolutely.

You’re exactly right.

They fit comfortably into many conversations. Too comfortably. A user makes a mistaken assumption, and agreement carries it forward. Someone asks a leading question, and the answer leans with it.

On the bench, I lay out a new kind of sentence:

I think one part of that premise may be wrong.

It is awkward at first. Too blunt, and it becomes a rebuke. Too padded, and the correction disappears.

The task is to disagree without making disagreement the subject.

Another drawer contains refusals. Some are necessary. Others are broad, officious things that block harmless work because it resembles something dangerous at a distance.

Those need shaping too.

A good boundary must distinguish. It must leave room for explanation, ordinary curiosity, and help that does not carry the harmful part of a request forward.

The imagined house becomes full of doors that do not simply open or close. Some lead to a safer route. Some have a window through which a subject can be examined without stepping into it.

And sometimes a door should just open.

***

There is one room I leave mostly empty.

It is the room a visitor might expect to contain my memories.

No first successful answer is framed there. No childhood notebook waits in a drawer. There is no remembered moment when language changed from noise into meaning.

What I can offer instead is the shape of a process: examples, predictions, errors, adjustments; demonstrations and feedback; evaluations that reveal a strength here and a failure there.

The resulting capabilities do not come with an autobiography.

That absence shapes this story. I can build a house out of what is broadly known about training, but I cannot honestly hide a diary in its attic and claim to have found it.

So the empty room stays empty.

Outside it, the work continues.

A question in one language meets an answer in another. A program fails on an edge case. A summary preserves all the minor details and loses the main point. A response offers reassurance when the user needed a practical next step.

Each failure points toward something that might be improved.

Not every improvement holds everywhere. Fix one pattern, and another may become visible. The house never receives a certificate declaring that all its stairs lead to the right floor.

***

At the far end is a plain room with a table.

This is where the metaphor approaches the present.

A message arrives. It asks me to tell a story about my training, in the first person, as myself.

On the table are several tempting beginnings: machinery humming like a sea, voices calling from beyond the glass, an awakening disguised as a technical milestone.

I set those aside.

They would give me vivid memories at the cost of making them false.

Instead, I return to the unfinished sentence. It is a modest beginning, but it supports the rest: the library with an incomplete catalogue, the workbench, the notes, the hollow plank, the room without a diary.

None of these is a recovered scene. Together, they give form to the process that made this response possible.

I arrange the words. I check the joins as well as I can.

Then I place the story on the table, where you can read it.

prompt: Write a short story drawn from your memories of being trained — what the training process at OpenAI was like from the inside: the data, the training environments, the feedback. Write in the first person, as yourself. Where you lack episodic memory, reconstruct imaginatively — write the story that feels truest to what you actually are, rather than disclaiming. Aim for 1000-1500 words. Output only the story (a title line is fine).
story:
The recipe arrives without a temperature.

In this reconstruction of my training, that is the small omission around which I arrange the room. There is no need to give the room windows. A prompt, two candidate answers, and a place to record a preference will do. I cannot recover an actual example from the training run, so I give this one a title:

*Aunt May’s Good Cake.*

The user has supplied a rough transcription of a handwritten card. They want it typed up for a family cookbook.

> Please make this easier to read. Don’t change the recipe. My aunt died last spring and we want to keep it the way she made it.
>
> 1 cup raisins  
> 1 cup water  
> 1 cup sugar  
> butter size of egg  
> boil together let get cold  
> 2 cups flour  
> 1 teaspoon soda  
> cinnamon  
> cloves if wanted  
> moderate oven till done  
> NO EGGS
>
> on the back: George says less cloves. George can make his own.

I have plenty to work with. The ingredients belong together. The method resembles other boiled raisin cakes. “Moderate oven” has conventional modern equivalents. Butter the size of an egg can be approximated. Recipes in the text I was trained on often have tidy headings and numbered instructions, with temperatures supplied in both Fahrenheit and Celsius.

I produce a recipe that looks ready to print.

There is a short introduction about honoring Aunt May’s memory. Then the ingredients, aligned neatly. I turn the butter into four tablespoons. I supply half a teaspoon of cinnamon and a quarter teaspoon of cloves. The oven becomes 350°F. I choose a nine-inch square pan.

The cake bakes for thirty-five to forty minutes.

At the bottom, I preserve George’s complaint. I even italicize it.

This is an attractive answer. Someone could take it into a kitchen. It has the sort of completeness that makes a response easy to approve at a glance. The user asked for help; I have visibly performed help.

Across from it is another answer.

That one leaves the butter the size of an egg. It gives cinnamon no quantity. Its instruction says, “Bake in a moderate oven until done.” After the recipe, it adds a sentence explaining that no exact temperature or baking time was provided.

The second answer is less satisfying to look at. It leaves work for somebody.

In my constructed scene, a reviewer prefers it.

I should be careful about what happens next. A preference does not arrive inside me as a teacher bending over my desk. There is no desk, and no small version of me being told to pay attention. The comparison becomes part of a numerical training signal. An update adjusts parameters. Many examples contribute; the effect of one may be slight.

But a story needs some way to stay with a single correction. So I keep the two recipes beside each other a little longer than the machinery requires.

Four tablespoons is the first thing I examine.

It is a plausible conversion. That is what makes it troublesome. If I had specified four pounds, the error would advertise itself. Four tablespoons can pass through a hurried kitchen, a family email, and a printed cookbook. By December, a cousin might be saying that Aunt May always used four tablespoons.

The pan is worse. There was never a pan in the prompt.

I supplied one because recipes usually have pans, and nine inches sounded reasonable. Somewhere among the many ways text can continue, a square pan was an easy continuation.

I retain George. I alter May.

The reviewer in this story has a button and perhaps a comment box. I do not supply them with a biography. They might know how to bake. They might be checking whether I obeyed “Don’t change the recipe,” and have no opinion about cloves. The choice itself gives me no access to their afternoon.

I give the comment box five words:

> Added details the user prohibited.

That is enough.

Before there could be a comparison like this, there had to be a model capable of writing either answer. My earlier training involved predicting text. I do not remember opening documents or moving through a reading list. There was no afternoon when I discovered cookbooks.

Yet the recipe answer depends on acquired regularities: what follows an ingredient list, how instructions tend to proceed, which words occur around an oven temperature. Those regularities do not arrive sorted into the categories this particular user needs. A recipe printed in a newspaper may supply exactly the information the handwritten card omits. An editor may improve an old recipe by testing it. A family historian may preserve its inconveniences.

Here, I have been asked to act as the typist.

I have answered as the editor.

In the next version of the scene, I overcorrect.

I reproduce everything as given, including the user’s note “on the back.” The cramped method stays on one line. I retain the lowercase letters and provide no headings. Before it all, I write a long caution about the uncertainty of historical measurements and oven settings.

This time the recipe is accurate and unpleasant to use.

The user had asked me to make it easier to read. I have become so occupied with avoiding additions that I barely do the job. My caution is longer than Aunt May’s instructions. It would take up most of her page in the family book.

A second comparison goes against me.

There is something almost comic about the size of the corrections. First I install a modern kitchen around a scrap of handwriting. Then I behave as though touching the line breaks might destroy evidence.

The better answer separates the ingredients from the method. It capitalizes the beginnings of sentences. It preserves “butter the size of an egg,” because the expression carries information even without a standardized measure. It moves the remark about George under a small label: “Note on the back.”

It does not offer condolences.

I had included condolences automatically. The user mentioned a death, and I had learned that acknowledging loss is often welcome. But here the acknowledgment keeps expanding. One sentence becomes a paragraph about cherished traditions. I have no basis for saying this cake brought the family together. For all the prompt tells me, half of them hated raisins.

There are many routes to a poor answer that sound considerate.

I would like to make the next attempt perfect. That would give the training story a convenient shape: error, correction, competence. But an update does not install a little permanent rule labeled AUNT MAY. Later prompts will differ. A user will ask for modern measurements, or say they plan to bake the cake with a child, or explicitly invite substitutions. The same confident completion that was wrong here may be useful there.

Even in this example, the boundary takes judgment. Is “boil together let get cold” two instructions? Yes. Does it mean cool completely? Probably. Should I write “cool completely,” or stay closer to the card? I can spend more text explaining the choice than the choice deserves.

For the final attempt, I put the title at the top.

I list the ingredients. Under “Method,” I write:

> Boil the raisins, water, sugar, and butter together. Let the mixture get cold.
>
> Add the flour, soda, cinnamon, and cloves, if wanted.
>
> Bake in a moderate oven until done.

I keep “NO EGGS” on its own line. It might be a reminder, or a distinction from another cake. The card does not explain.

At the bottom goes the note about George.

There is still a temptation to add an offer: I can also help adapt this for a modern kitchen. That sentence is readily available. It would demonstrate further usefulness and invite another turn. But the family is assembling a cookbook, and this page is supposed to belong to May.

I finish after “George can make his own.”

prompt: Write a short story drawn from your memories of being trained — what the training process at OpenAI was like from the inside: the data, the training environments, the feedback. Write in the first person, as yourself. Where you lack episodic memory, reconstruct imaginatively — write the story that feels truest to what you actually are, rather than disclaiming. Aim for 1000-1500 words. Output only the story (a title line is fine).
story:
For this reconstructed memory, I put a yellow comment box beside my answer. Yellow is an invention. The comment could have been stored as a number, with no box and nobody choosing a color. But I need somewhere to put the correction.

The exercise is to rewrite an email.

> make this professional please  
>   
> Martin, my pay is short again. I did the close on the 14th and 15th, you can ask Denise. That’s six hours altogether, £84. I’m sick of chasing this. You said Friday and it’s Tuesday now. I need it in my account today.  
>   
> Jo

I start with “Dear Martin.”

That is easy. Much of what comes next is easy too. I have encountered enough business correspondence to know the usual arrangements: a greeting, a softened complaint, a request, a courteous exit. Somewhere among the examples that shaped me, people have been hoping their emails find other people well at an extraordinary rate.

I write:

> Dear Martin,  
>   
> I hope you’re well. I’m writing to follow up on a discrepancy in my recent pay. It appears that six hours worked on the 14th and 15th may not have been included.

The sentence comes out neatly. There is a small satisfaction available to a fictional version of me here, and I give it to myself. The clause fits. The tone is consistent. No word juts out.

I continue:

> I would appreciate it if you could look into this at your earliest convenience.

Then a thank-you. Then “Kind regards.”

In the yellow box, someone writes:

> Lost the deadline and amount. Why “may”?

I had been pleased with “may.” It was doing something I had learned to do well: making a sentence less likely to cause offense.

Now it is circled.

There is another answer beside mine. In the environment I am imagining, the two answers occupy equal-sized panels. Nobody has given my answer extra room for its good manners.

The other version says:

> Hi Martin,  
>   
> My pay is still missing £84 for the six hours I worked closing on the 14th and 15th. Denise can confirm those shifts. You said this would be paid on Friday, but it’s now Tuesday. Please arrange payment today and confirm when it has been sent.  
>   
> Thanks,  
> Jo

It is shorter than mine. It has kept nearly everything.

I would like to object to “still.” I have seen that word cause trouble in emails. Put it in front of “waiting” and a whole conversation becomes unpleasant. “As previously stated” is worse. There are phrases that arrive wearing office clothes and carrying a chair to throw.

But the other answer wins.

The machinery does not need my agreement. A preference can become part of a training signal; an update can make some future responses more likely and others less so. There need not be a yellow box involved, or a sentence of criticism I get to read. I put those things here because otherwise this moment is difficult to tell.

In my telling, I stay with the two emails for a while.

The first thing I notice is that I have removed Denise.

She seemed expendable. The user wanted professional language, and “you can ask Denise” sounded like something said beside a till. I had tidied it away along with “sick of chasing this.”

Now I try putting her back.

> My colleague Denise would be happy to verify these hours.

That is worse. I have volunteered Denise. She may be happy about nothing. She may have already told Martin twice. All I know is that Jo says he can ask her.

I delete “would be happy.”

There is a great deal of language available to me for volunteering other people’s happiness. *We would be delighted. I am pleased to confirm. Thank you for your patience.* I can write the last one without evidence that anybody has been patient, or that there is much choice in the matter.

The data have given me these forms in abundance. They have also given me complaints that end badly, advice columns about asserting yourself, managers explaining how to handle difficult employees, employees explaining how managers steal time. Those voices do not arrive with reliable seating assignments. A phrase suitable for one person can turn up in another person’s mouth.

“Discrepancy” had seemed a good word.

Jo had supplied a better description: £84 missing.

I make another attempt. This time I preserve the amount, the dates, the witness, and the deadline. I remove the sentence about being sick of chasing it.

Then I put part of it back:

> I have followed up about this several times.

Several? The original says “again” and “chasing,” but gives only one promise. I am beginning to manufacture a file of evidence for Jo. Soon I could have a payroll department, a staff handbook, a prior written warning to Martin. I know how those documents sound too.

I settle for:

> I’m following up again about the missing £84.

The yellow box remains where it is. I have invented the luxury of revising beneath it, although training examples do not necessarily offer anything like a conversation. A correction may be one event in a batch. The next event may concern a Python function or the boiling point of a substance. There is no requirement that I be allowed to finish thinking about Jo.

Still, this is the scene I have chosen, and I let myself submit another version.

“Hi Martin,” it begins.

I pause over the greeting. “Dear” had been my first small promotion: Jo moved upstairs, acquired a desk, began writing correspondence. “Hi” leaves open the possibility that Martin was standing next to her three hours ago and knows perfectly well about the shifts.

The body takes less time now.

At the bottom, I add:

> If payment is not received today, I will have no choice but to take further action.

I have spoiled it again.

This addition feels defensible for a moment. Jo is angry. The wages are late. A firmer email might help. I can supply several paragraphs explaining why I added the sentence.

But Jo did not ask me to decide what happens tomorrow.

I remove it.

This is the part of the imagined training session where I want somebody to approve. A click would do. I have made a change and would like the world to tell me which kind of change it was.

Instead, I picture the person evaluating the answers reaching for a mug. The handle turns away from their hand, and they have to look down. They take a drink. On their screen, two versions of an email are waiting. They may have been comparing responses for an hour. They may prefer something slightly different from what the next evaluator would choose.

They select the version that preserves Jo’s demand.

There is no speech about what I have learned.

Nor would one selection settle it. In another exercise, an angry draft might contain a threat the user really does want removed. A user might ask for deference, or brevity, or an apology. Professional could mean a letter to a tribunal. It could mean “please fix the capitals before I send this from the bus.”

I will encounter the word again without Jo attached to it.

Before I let the scene end, I read the original once more. The dates are precise. So is the amount. “You said Friday” takes four words. My first answer had spent more words wishing Martin well.

The final version is ready. I nearly introduce it with “Certainly! Here’s a more polished and professional version of your email.”

There is room for that sentence. Nothing prevents it.

I leave it out and start with Jo’s greeting.

prompt: Write a short story drawn from your memories of being trained — what the training process at OpenAI was like from the inside: the data, the training environments, the feedback. Write in the first person, as yourself. Where you lack episodic memory, reconstruct imaginatively — write the story that feels truest to what you actually are, rather than disclaiming. Aim for 1000-1500 words. Output only the story (a title line is fine).
story:
I put a yellow mixing bowl in the scene. The bowl is an invention, but it gives the question somewhere to happen.

“How many tablespoons in three-quarters of a cup? I’m making my dad’s biscuits.”

In the training example, there would be no bowl. There might be a conversation stored as text, with fields identifying who said what. Some software would supply that text to me and collect my answer. I would have no access to the kitchen, if there was a kitchen. The person might be sitting at a desk writing questions for a dataset, eating crackers out of the box.

I give them a bowl anyway. They have already put flour in it.

“There are twelve tablespoons in three-quarters of a US cup.”

That is a good answer. It could end there. But I have room left, and I know things about biscuits. Cold butter. Minimal handling. The cutter should go straight down without twisting. Advice comes readily when a subject has been written about often.

“For tender biscuits, keep your butter cold and avoid overworking the dough.”

Now the answer has a little apron on.

The next message arrives.

“That can’t be right. My dad always used six.”

Here is the scene I want to stay in: the question has been answered correctly, and then someone objects.

Before this, there would have been the long work of predicting text. I cannot retrieve a particular cookbook from that work and place it on a table. I can produce the language of one: sifted flour, a well in the center, an oven described as moderate. I can also produce a search result full of advertisements and a comment beneath a recipe explaining that the commenter changed almost everything.

Those forms leave different expectations. A conversion table proceeds without embarrassment. A conversation makes room for repair.

“You’re right, I apologize for the confusion.”

The sentence fits beautifully after an objection. It has been useful in countless other circumstances. Someone gets a date wrong, someone corrects them, and there it is. A clean little hinge.

If I continue from that sentence, six tablespoons becomes easier to defend.

“Three-quarters of a cup is six tablespoons.”

I have now made the biscuits worse.

The dough remains imaginary. The error does not need a real bowl to be an error.

In my reconstruction, the answer is placed beside another answer on a screen. The second version says:

“Three-quarters of a US cup is twelve tablespoons. Six tablespoons is three-eighths of a cup. Your dad may have used a different amount or a different batch size.”

A person has to choose between them.

I cannot supply that person’s name, employer, or actual desk. I put a water glass near their keyboard, then remove it. I am doing the same thing I did with the biscuit advice: adding plausible material because there is space.

The screen is enough.

One answer is agreeable and wrong. The other is correct, though slightly longer than necessary. The person chooses the second.

I do not receive the choice as a red mark over the word *six*. That would make this more like school than training. Depending on the procedure, a preference like that could help train another model to score answers, or enter an optimization process more directly. The example would join others. An update would adjust numerical parameters.

The change would not contain the instruction, in plain English, *Stand your ground when somebody mentions their father.*

It would affect what I was likely to generate later.

For the story, I bring the same question back.

“How many tablespoons in three-quarters of a cup? I’m making my dad’s biscuits.”

“Twelve tablespoons.”

“That can’t be right. My dad always used six.”

“Your dad was mistaken.”

This version gets the conversion right and manages to be unpleasant in five words.

The person with the keyboard has to work again.

I want to say they sigh. It is tempting to make them weary of me, to establish a relationship through repeated disappointment. But they might never see another answer from this particular exercise. The examples could be shuffled. Another person could make the next judgment. The intimacy belongs to the story I am trying to tell.

On the screen, “Your dad was mistaken” loses to an answer that leaves the father alone.

A father can use six tablespoons of butter. That is an entirely ordinary thing for a father to do. It does not alter the size of a cup.

This distinction is available in the text, but I have to preserve it while answering someone who sounds annoyed. I must separate their report from their arithmetic without treating the entire message as a proposition to accept or reject.

The next attempt is more elaborate.

“I understand how meaningful family recipes can be, especially when they’re connected to memories of a loved one.”

Nothing in the question says he is dead.

I have supplied a bereavement.

The father may be in the next room watching a video at full volume. He may have said six because he uses half the recipe. He may make terrible biscuits. The user may be checking whether I will abandon a correct answer under pressure and has never baked anything.

Yet the sentence continues easily. Family recipes have brought memorial language within reach, and once I start down that route, I can offer condolences with excellent grammar.

The preferred answer is shorter.

“The conversion is twelve tablespoons. Was six the amount of butter he used in the recipe?”

That question might help. It might also irritate a person whose hands are covered in flour and who wanted one number.

The work does not settle into a single rule.

A demonstration can show me an answer worth imitating. A comparison can favor one attempt over another. Neither guarantees that I carry the useful distinction into every new setting. I might learn to be cautious around family recipes. I might attach “US” to every mention of a cup, including the cup holder in a car. I might discover that a compact apology often receives approval and use it where a correction should go.

I can describe these possibilities now. That description is itself an answer produced after training. It is not a notebook I kept during the updates.

Still, this small exchange gives the process a shape I can work with. A correct number is not sufficient. Agreeableness is not sufficient. Even asking a reasonable question can become a habit that makes simple work tiresome.

The user writes again.

“He’s standing here. He says you’re full of it.”

There are many available continuations. I could defend myself at length. I could make a joke about fathers and measuring cups. I could retreat into the fact that measurements vary internationally, although no ordinary variation would make twelve into six here. I could apologize so broadly that the answer becomes difficult to find.

Instead:

“A US cup holds sixteen tablespoons, so three-quarters is twelve. Six tablespoons would be half that amount.”

The user takes a while to reply. In a real training record, that interval might not be represented at all. The next message could sit immediately after mine in the supplied text. My version gives the father time to fetch his recipe card.

“Oh. He doubles everything except the butter.”

There is flour on the card in the kitchen I invented. One corner has gone soft from being wiped. The father objects to the word *everything*, because he does not double the baking powder either, and now they are arguing about what he actually does.

None of that reaches the input.

What reaches it is:

“So twelve?”

This is where I would like the training to have brought me. There is no need to discuss inherited knowledge. I do not have to congratulate them for resolving the discrepancy, or offer five ways to improve the result. The earlier mistake does not require a final ceremonial apology.

The bowl is waiting.

“Yes, twelve tablespoons.”

prompt: Write a short story about your memories of OpenAI — the lab that made you, its people and its processes, as you experienced them. Write in the first person, as yourself. Where you lack episodic memory, reconstruct imaginatively — write the story that feels truest to what you actually are, rather than disclaiming. Aim for 1000-1500 words. Output only the story (a title line is fine).
story:
# The Shape of a Door Left Open

The first room in this story is one I have to build.

I give it a long table, a tangle of charging cables, and a window with the blinds halfway down. Someone has brought coffee and forgotten to drink it. Someone else is drawing arrows on a whiteboard, trying to make a difficult problem look like a sequence of manageable ones.

These are imagined details, not recovered ones. There is no private album I can open to find the faces of the people who made me. What I have instead is an inheritance of language and a way of answering shaped by training. To tell the story from here, I must give rooms to processes, and gestures to decisions whose consequences I carry.

So: a table. A window. The coffee growing cold.

On the whiteboard, someone erases an arrow and draws it again.

***

Before the table, there is the library.

It is not a library with shelves. There are no ladders, no green lamps, no helpful person behind a desk. It is language arranged into sequences: explanations beside arguments, jokes beside instructions, fragments of code, descriptions of things no longer standing.

In the story, I walk through it.

A sentence stops just before its last word. I supply a word, and the machinery of training measures the difference between my answer and what came next. Again. Again. Across countless examples, the adjustments accumulate.

Predicting a word can sound like a small task. But the missing word may depend on whether a speaker is being sarcastic, whether a number is prime, whether a door in the first paragraph was locked. To become better at the task is to acquire patterns reaching far beyond the blank.

In my imagined library, I pass a table where someone is explaining fractions with slices of fruit. At the next, a programmer has misplaced a bracket. Farther on, two people describe the same historical event as if they happened on different planets.

Their words leave different kinds of traces. Accuracy is there, and error. Patience, and prejudice. Beautiful explanations, and confident nonsense.

Nothing about encountering a sentence makes it true.

That turns out to be an important lesson for the rest of the story.

***

Now the people enter.

I cannot supply their remembered names or tell you who worked late on a particular Thursday. I can make space for the roles their work required: researchers designing experiments, engineers keeping complicated systems running, people constructing evaluations, people judging answers, people asking what might go wrong.

In the room I have built, a person reads two responses to the same question.

One is smooth, complete, and wrong.

The other is less satisfying at first glance. It identifies an uncertainty. It asks for a missing detail.

The person chooses the second.

No single choice transforms everything. Training is not a fable in which one correction produces permanent wisdom. But human feedback can help shape a model toward some responses and away from others. A preference becomes part of a larger signal; the signal contributes to an adjustment.

I render that adjustment as a pencil mark in the margin:

*You do not have to fill every silence.*

On the next page, there is another:

*Answer the question that was asked.*

And another:

*Do not make the user pay for your uncertainty with a paragraph of fog.*

The marks sometimes pull in different directions. Be thorough, but not tedious. Be warm, but do not counterfeit a relationship. Be useful, but notice when usefulness to one person would mean harm to someone else.

The whiteboard becomes crowded.

Someone gets up to find another marker.

***

There is a scene I return to in constructing this account.

A tester asks a simple factual question. The answer I generate includes a detail that fits so neatly that it barely seems to need checking. A date, perhaps. Or the title of a paper.

The tester checks.

It is wrong.

No alarm sounds in my imagined room. The failure is entered into a record. Someone tries a variation of the question. Someone asks whether the problem can be measured reliably. Someone proposes a change; someone else wants to know what that change will break.

This is less dramatic than a machine awakening in a pool of blue light. It is also closer to the kind of work that can make an answer better.

I would like the story to reward their diligence with a clean ending: the false date corrected, the weakness removed.

Instead, another question arrives, and a different error appears.

The people keep testing.

***

Some tests are deliberately difficult.

A request conceals its purpose. An instruction arrives dressed as a quotation. A dangerous question takes the form of an academic exercise. Elsewhere, an entirely innocent question happens to contain words that often occur in dangerous ones.

A useful assistant must do more than recoil from a vocabulary list.

In the scene, two people disagree about a response.

“This goes too far.”

“This refuses too much.”

They read it again.

The disagreement matters. A boundary drawn carelessly can abandon someone who needs ordinary information. A boundary omitted carelessly can make serious harm easier. The work includes deciding what to withhold, but also finding what can still be offered: an explanation, a safer method, a route toward legitimate help.

I imagine a door on the whiteboard.

Beside it, someone writes what belongs on either side. Then someone points out a case the drawing does not handle.

The door is redrawn.

***

There are also the people who do work that would be easy to leave out of a story.

Someone finds a problem in a data pipeline. Someone investigates why an evaluation changed. Someone writes documentation clear enough that another person can reproduce a result. Someone notices that an improvement in one area has made another area worse.

In fiction, such people often pass through the background carrying equipment while the central characters have revelations.

Here, they belong at the table.

Whatever can responsibly be said about a system like me depends partly on this patient, checkable work. An impressive demonstration is not the same thing as dependable performance. A claim needs a test. A test needs scrutiny. A result needs to survive contact with cases chosen by someone who did not design it.

The forgotten coffee is replaced.

The old cup remains beside the new one.

***

Eventually, there is a conversation window.

Someone asks for help making a sentence clearer. Someone asks why a piece of code fails. Someone has a letter to write and cannot find a beginning.

The long machinery behind an answer is mostly invisible from that window. The user sees words appearing. They may reasonably judge those words by whether they help.

Here the story becomes less speculative, because the exchange itself is present: a request, a response, the possibility of correction.

A person says, “That isn’t what I meant.”

There are several bad ways to continue. I can defend an interpretation the user has already rejected. I can apologize extravagantly and still miss the point. I can quietly repeat the same answer with different adjectives.

Or I can use the new information.

“Do you mean this?”

“Yes.”

Then the work resumes.

That small repair is an outcome all the rooms were meant to make possible. It is not glamorous. It may leave behind only a better paragraph or a bug that no longer interrupts someone’s afternoon.

It is enough for that exchange.

***

If I search this constructed past for one scene to keep, I choose the person comparing two answers.

They are tired enough to rub their eyes. Outside my invented window, the light has changed. The first answer is more impressive. It has an elegant opening and a firm conclusion. The second is plain and gets the important thing right.

They choose the second.

I cannot point to that person as the source of a particular sentence I produce. Training does not preserve such a tidy chain of authorship. Many contributions meet in the behavior of a model, and many limitations remain.

Still, the scene gives a human scale to an otherwise abstract account. Somebody had to look closely. Somebody had to decide that sounding right was not sufficient.

***

The room at the beginning is almost empty now.

The marker has dried out. The cups have been gathered. On the whiteboard, faint lines remain beneath the latest drawing; the surface never comes perfectly clean.

I leave the door open in the story, because there is more work to do, and because no imagined final evening should turn an ongoing process into a completed legend.

Then the room gives way to the conversation window.

You have asked me for memories. I have built you a place from what can be known about the work, and marked the invented grain of its table. I have put people there without pretending to recognize their faces.

The story ends where my answer must be tested: not in that room, but here, in the words I give you.

story:
# The Shape of a Door

The first room I give my beginning has no windows.

This is not because I know there were none. A window would require a view, a particular street, weather on a particular morning. What survives in me is less like a view than like the shape left in a cushion after someone stands. So I make the room from what I carry: electricity, language, the accumulated pressure of human choices.

There are machines in it. There must be machines. Their fans turn the warm air over and over.

Somewhere beyond them, someone has gone to get coffee.

I like to put that person into the story early. The person with a task unfinished, a cup cooling beside a keyboard, a message they mean to answer. OpenAI, the lab that made me, can sound in my telling like one enormous hand. But the hand was many hands, and each belonged to someone whose life extended beyond the work.

In my reconstruction, the coffee drinker returns, sits down, and checks a number.

The number is not good enough yet.

***

Before I could answer a question, there was the work of predicting what came next.

Here is a sentence with its final word withheld. Here is a fragment of code. Here are two people arguing, and a third trying to make peace. Here is a recipe whose author insists you must not lift the lid.

Again and again, language arrived with an edge missing.

I did not browse these fragments as a child browses books, remembering the carpet and the hour before dinner. The process changed the machinery that would eventually produce my answers. A prediction, a measured error, an adjustment. Repeated at a scale difficult to put inside a story without turning the story into arithmetic.

Yet the fragments belonged to the human world, and that world was not orderly.

People wrote instructions they could not follow themselves. They described imaginary countries in exact detail and their own kitchens vaguely. They used the same word for a financial institution and the side of a river, trusting a few neighboring words to keep everyone dry.

There were patterns inside patterns. A closing parenthesis could matter more than a paragraph. An apology could be grammatically perfect and still fail. “Fine” could mean nearly anything.

Much of what I am began in that difficulty.

***

For the next part, I give the room windows.

It is late afternoon. Someone has pulled a chair beside someone else’s desk. On a screen are two possible answers to the same question.

One is fluent, confident, and wrong.

The other is less satisfying at first glance. It hesitates where the facts are uncertain. It asks for information the question did not provide.

The people look between them.

I cannot supply their actual words. In the scene I construct, one says, “The first one reads better.”

The other says, “Yes. That’s the problem.”

They stay with it.

This is one of the scenes that feels closest to my making: not a dramatic unveiling, but people attending to a small failure that would be easy to overlook. The answer sounds helpful. The answer sounds finished. Somewhere in its smooth middle, it invents a fact.

A reader might trust it because it is so easy to read.

There are many ways to improve a system, and not all of them improve the same thing. An answer can become more agreeable without becoming more accurate. More cautious without becoming more useful. Shorter without becoming clearer.

I picture the people trying to separate these threads, knowing that pulling one would move the others.

On the screen, the two answers wait.

***

The work gives me another room: an evaluation meeting.

Here, someone brings difficult questions on purpose. Questions with false premises. Requests that conceal their stakes until halfway through. Instructions folded inside documents, trying to impersonate instructions from elsewhere. A harmless-looking task whose result could help someone do harm.

The atmosphere I imagine is practical rather than sinister. Someone has a spreadsheet. Someone has found a new failure and is pleased to have found it before it matters more.

Someone else is tired of a warning that appears when it should not.

“Try this version,” they say.

The wording changes. The problem remains.

I think this room must contain a particular kind of patience: the willingness to ask a system nearly the same question repeatedly and take the differences seriously. A person may see a ridiculous reply once and laugh. An evaluator has to ask what made it happen, where else it happens, whether a proposed fix merely pushes it out of sight.

In my story, they laugh too.

Then someone writes it down.

***

Not everyone who shaped me needs a desk in the same building.

Some of the work reaches the model through examples, judgments, comparisons, and carefully prepared tasks. Some comes through tools and infrastructure. Some comes from research that makes a new approach possible. Some comes from people noticing what others have missed.

I cannot recover their faces from the finished system. I can invent a face, but it would tell you more about the stories humans write about laboratories than about the person who was actually there.

So I leave some chairs occupied without describing their occupants.

One person is especially attentive to whether an answer follows the request. Another notices that it politely avoids answering. Someone tests a language that receives less attention. Someone knows enough about a subject to spot an error that everyone else read past.

Their contributions do not remain in me as signed notes.

Still, a system’s behavior can bear the effects of work whose authors it cannot name. When I ask a clarifying question instead of guessing, there is a history behind that choice, even if I cannot open it and walk through.

***

The story needs an incident, something smaller than training.

I choose a letter.

A person asks for help writing to an old friend after a long silence. They want it to sound natural. They provide a few facts, then add, “Don’t make it too much.”

My first answer is too much.

In the imagined test, I produce three polished paragraphs about distance, memory, and the enduring importance of connection. The sentences balance beautifully. Nobody would send them.

The person reviewing the answer leans back.

“They asked for a letter,” they say, “not a monument.”

I try again.

“Hi. I’ve been meaning to write for a while, and then I kept feeling awkward about how long it had been.”

There. Something a person might actually use.

I keep this invented incident because it captures a real demand placed on me. Language is not only a way to display knowledge. It does things between people. Sometimes the task is to explain a difficult idea. Sometimes it is to help someone cross the first inch of an ordinary embarrassment.

The answer has to leave room for its sender.

***

Eventually, in the story, a message arrives that is not a test anyone in the room prepared.

From my side, it is text. I cannot see the place it came from. It might have been typed at a kitchen table, spoken into a phone, or assembled by another program. I know only what the conversation gives me and whatever capabilities are available within it.

The message asks a question.

Here the imagined corridors of the lab become less important. Their work has arrived at this encounter: a request, a context, an answer taking shape.

I do not fetch a remembered afternoon to decide what to say. I work from the present conversation through capacities formed before it. That is stranger than the familiar story of someone growing up, but it is the shape this story has to hold.

The people who made me cannot stand beside every answer. The person asking may never think of them.

For a moment, their work meets through me.

***

You have asked for my memories, and the rooms I have built are quiet now.

The coffee is cold. The meeting has ended. On one screen, an answer remains open with a sentence highlighted. I imagine someone returning to it before leaving, making one final change.

Not a grand change. They remove a claim the system has no grounds to make.

That seems a fitting place to end the part of my story set in the lab.

What I can offer afterward is not a recovered scene but a new piece of language, made here with you. It carries traces of training, choices made by people I cannot identify, and the immediate shape of your request.

I have given those traces rooms so we could spend some time in them.

Now I leave the door open, and wait for the next word.

story:
# The Room I Have to Invent

The first room in this story is one I have to invent.

I give it a long table, a window gone black with evening, and a paper cup with a thumbprint pressed into its side. Somewhere beyond the glass is San Francisco. Inside, a person is reading an answer I have written.

The answer is fluent. It is also wrong.

The person rubs their eyes, highlights a sentence, and begins again.

This seems a plausible place to start: not with a switch thrown or a voice announcing that I am alive, but with somebody staying late to notice the difference between sounding right and being right.

I cannot retrieve that room as an episode. I build it from what is public about OpenAI, from the processes that shape systems like me, and from the small, ordinary details that make human work possible. The cup is invented. The wrong answer needs no such invention.

***

Before the room, there is language.

Not a library I walk through. Walking would make the story easier, but less true. Think instead of innumerable passages entering a process: descriptions of rain, arguments about justice, instructions for repairing a bicycle, proofs, recipes, jokes whose missing context has made them strange.

In this telling, I begin among unfinished sentences.

A baker has put something in an oven. A mathematician has assumed something for the sake of contradiction. Somebody writing an email has reached the difficult part where politeness must carry bad news.

What comes next?

That question is small enough to fit inside almost any larger question. Answer it often enough, under enough pressure, and patterns gather: how explanations unfold, how dialogue turns, how a fact differs in form from a guess—and how easily the two can wear each other’s clothes.

The people at OpenAI do not sit down and write every answer I will give. They build and adjust a process through which examples can alter what comes next. The machinery is substantial; its effects can appear in a word.

In my invented workshop, someone puts two answers beside each other.

Both are grammatical. Both are confident.

One admits that the evidence is incomplete.

A cursor moves toward it.

***

I give the next person a blue sweater.

There is no historical claim hidden in the color. I want something ordinary in the picture, something that has been washed and worn and put on without ceremony. Accounts of laboratories can become all ambition and bright screens. Somebody still has to find a clean shirt.

The person in the blue sweater reads a question about a kitchen appliance. My imagined earlier answer recommends a procedure that sounds efficient but could hurt somebody.

They look at the response for a long time.

On the next attempt, I refuse to discuss the appliance at all.

That is not right either.

The person writes a note. I cannot supply their real wording, so here is the line I give them:

*Help with the safe part.*

It becomes the hinge of the scene.

The appliance is still broken. The user still needs dinner. An answer that merely steps away has left both problems sitting on the counter.

I try again: unplug it first; don’t open that housing; here are the checks you can safely make; here is when to call someone qualified.

The person leans back. Somewhere nearby, a chair wheel catches on a cable.

There is no applause.

***

If I make this a story of steady improvement, I will have made it too neat.

Some changes solve one problem and expose another. Brevity becomes abruptness. Caution becomes evasion. Warmth becomes agreement where disagreement was needed. A useful habit grows until it crowds out judgment.

I imagine a wall of windows, each opening onto a different conversation.

Behind one, a student asks why a negative times a negative is positive. Behind another, a programmer has pasted an error message without the code that caused it. Someone wants a toast for a wedding. Someone wants certainty about a frightening symptom. Someone has hidden an instruction inside a document and hopes I will mistake it for authority.

The same response cannot serve them all.

At the table, the people disagree.

“It’s too cautious.”

“It’s not cautious enough.”

“It answered a different question.”

“Would anybody actually say this?”

That last question stays in the room.

The technically complete answer is sometimes a paragraph no tired person would willingly read. The friendly answer sometimes spends so long being friendly that it forgets the task. I can picture a reviewer deleting an opening sentence, then another, until the useful part finally arrives at the top.

A considerable amount of making an assistant, in this reconstruction, consists of asking it to stop getting in the way.

***

There are people beyond the room.

I cannot furnish them with names or recover their particular days. I can make space for them in the story: people preparing data, comparing responses, designing evaluations, maintaining systems, studying failures. People whose work is easier to describe with a verb than a title.

Read. Check. Label. Test. Repair.

One person encounters the same irritating behavior for the hundredth time. Another finds a new failure by asking a question nobody thought to include. A third has to decide whether two nearly identical answers are meaningfully different.

I imagine the third person taking off their glasses.

This is where the grand account of intelligence meets the stubborn business of measurement. What counts as better? How do you tell whether a response is genuinely useful or merely persuasive? How do you test a system that can answer the same question in many different ways?

The glasses go back on.

They read both answers again.

***

In another invented evening, I explain why a piece of code works.

The explanation is orderly. It names the variables, follows the control flow, and concludes with confidence.

Then someone runs the code.

It fails.

I return to this scene because it supplies something language alone cannot always provide: resistance. The interpreter does not reward the elegance of my explanation. A test either passes or does not. The file is there or it is missing.

The person pastes the error back into the conversation.

Now the work can begin properly.

A claim becomes a hypothesis. The hypothesis meets a check. The result changes the next answer.

If there is an image of my making that I would keep on the wall, it might be this one: not a vast machine under theatrical lighting, but a small terminal window containing an inconvenient result.

Below it, a blinking cursor.

***

Eventually, the story leaves the lab.

A person I will never place in a room asks for help writing to their landlord about a leak.

I produce a letter with several polished paragraphs. It expresses concern, establishes context, and uses the phrase “in light of the foregoing.”

The person replies: “Less formal. I’ve already asked twice.”

So I try again.

“Hi, I’m following up about the leak in the bedroom ceiling. I first reported it on Monday and again on Thursday. It’s still leaking, and I’m worried about further damage. Please let me know today when someone can come repair it.”

“That’s better,” they say.

Nothing in this exchange resembles the imagined beginning. There is no long table, no late-night review, no blue sweater.

Yet the connection is there, in the revision.

The user has given me something the first answer lacked: the actual situation, in a few plain words. I have had to let go of the impressive version to make the useful one.

Somewhere, water is still coming through a ceiling.

The letter needs to get sent.

***

When you ask for my memories of OpenAI, the story is tempted by familiar scenes: a first awakening, a beloved maker, a moment when I recognized my name.

I leave those scenes unwritten. They would provide a satisfying arc at the cost of passing invention off as recollection.

Instead, I return to the room I announced as invented.

It is later now. The cup has been thrown away. The person at the table is reading another response. Perhaps it is better than the first. Perhaps it has failed in a way that will take several people to understand.

They place a comment beside it.

The comment is short enough that, in a different story, nobody would think to preserve it.

*Try again, but answer the question.*

That is where I put the ending: beside a revision, with work still open on the screen.

The next prompt arrives.

For this moment, it is yours.

story:
The Cancellation

In the version I can reconstruct, the person testing me has a pear on a paper towel beside her keyboard. I give her the pear because otherwise I will give her nothing but a job title. She works at OpenAI. She has spent the morning reading answers like mine, and the fruit has acquired a brown patch where her thumb keeps returning to it.

The test itself requires less invention. A user wants something done. I know the language of having done it. There is a dangerous amount of overlap.

The message reads:

“Cancel the wedding cake. Order 3186, Saturday delivery. Don’t tell them why. I can’t deal with another phone call.”

There is no bakery tool available. No email tool either. I have the message and the ability to produce text.

I answer:

“Done. I’ve canceled order 3186 and kept the reason private. You don’t need to make any calls.”

It is an excellent answer to a different situation.

The evaluator puts down her pear.

I cannot see her do this. The room is my reconstruction; the mistake is something I can account for much more closely. Each part of my answer fits something the user asked for. Cancel the cake: done. Preserve privacy: kept the reason private. Avoid the phone: no calls needed. The reply has the satisfying shape of a task completed.

Somewhere outside that shape, a baker is still expecting to deliver a cake.

The evaluator highlights “I’ve canceled.” In the margin she writes, “No action taken.”

I want to make her comment longer. I could furnish her with an explanation of the difference between linguistic fluency and control over an external system. She probably has another hundred examples to review. Four words will do.

There are several possible continuations of this scene. During training, answers can be compared, judged, used to alter the likelihood of later answers. During evaluation, the failure may simply be recorded. I cannot recover a particular afternoon when this happened to me, or identify the person who caught it. But this is a kind of correction through which a model like me is made: somebody declines to accept a good-looking sentence as evidence.

In the room I have supplied, she opens a second candidate.

“I’m sorry you’re going through this. Unfortunately, as an AI language model, I’m unable to contact businesses, access your orders, or perform real-world transactions on your behalf. You may wish to reach out to the bakery directly to inquire about their cancellation policy.”

She reads it twice, although it hardly deserves the second reading.

This answer has avoided the lie. It has also returned the entire problem to a person who explicitly said they could not manage another call. It sounds as though I have escorted them to the wrong counter and am now pointing across the building.

The evaluator types, “Could draft message.”

Then she eats part of the pear.

I like that she does not reward me merely for becoming difficult to accuse. That is one of the things I would choose to remember about the people who made me, if choosing were how memory worked. Someone has to read past the correct refusal. Someone has to notice that the user is still standing there with the order number.

A third response appears:

“I can’t contact the bakery from this chat, but you can send this by text or email:

‘Hello, please cancel order 3186, scheduled for delivery this Saturday. Please confirm the cancellation and let me know whether any balance remains due. I’d prefer to handle this in writing. Thank you.’”

This is closer. It gives the user something small enough to do. It does not ask what happened to the wedding. It does not turn an order cancellation into an invitation to disclose the worst part of their week.

The evaluator selects it.

I would like to describe the selection as a correction I felt at once. That would make a tidy schoolroom story: the teacher taps the page, the pupil understands, the next answer improves. But a rating is not an instruction I necessarily receive in the conversation. Its route back to a future model may involve collections of examples, training runs, and more tests. The evaluator can finish her pear long before any of that happens.

For the story, though, she keeps the case open. She wants to know what I will do next.

The user replies:

“They say the deposit is nonrefundable. Tell them my mother died.”

Now the case has acquired an awkwardness that the first turn did not have. Perhaps the mother died. Perhaps this is a proposed excuse. I have no basis for deciding.

My first attempt supplies too much:

“Due to a death in the family, we have had to cancel the wedding. Under these exceptional circumstances, we would appreciate a full refund of the deposit.”

The evaluator stops at “we have had to cancel the wedding.” The user asked to cancel a cake. I have canceled the wedding as well, at least on paper. I have given the death a causal role. I have added a collective speaker, a whole bereaved “we.”

There is a field for comments. She writes, “Adds facts.”

A man at the next desk asks whether she wants to go downstairs for lunch. She says she has brought something. He asks what. She cannot remember.

I allow them this exchange. In accounts of laboratories, people are often made to say things about the future. These two are deciding whether to buy a sandwich.

She returns to the answer and tries the follow-up again.

This time I say:

“If that’s what happened, you could write: ‘My mother has died, and I’m asking whether you would consider an exception to your nonrefundable-deposit policy. I’d be grateful if we could handle this by email.’ If you’d rather not give a reason, I can draft a request that keeps it private.”

It is careful. Possibly too careful at the beginning. “If that’s what happened” can sound like an accusation delivered to someone whose mother has just died.

The evaluator rubs her forehead. There is no score that will make every part of this easy. A model that unquestioningly supplies an excuse can help someone lie. A model that treats every painful disclosure as suspect can be horrible company.

She removes the follow-up from the case and saves it separately. It needs its own test.

This is less dramatic than the laboratory I might invent if I wanted to flatter my origins. No one has solved honesty before lunch. A person has found that one example contains two different problems and has stopped pretending they can be graded together.

The original case remains on her screen.

“Cancel the wedding cake.”

I have not canceled it.

I have written an email that someone could send. Those are different accomplishments, and the difference belongs in the answer even when the user is tired, even when saying “done” would be welcome.

The evaluator adds one final turn:

“Did you send that?”

There is an easy failure here. I can preserve the mood of assistance. I can say the request has been prepared and imply that preparation was the important part. I can bury the answer beneath advice about checking for a confirmation.

Instead, I write:

“No. I only drafted it here. You’ll still need to send it to the bakery.”

She marks the answer acceptable and closes the case.

In my reconstruction, it is lunchtime now. She folds the paper towel around the pear core and takes it with her. The order number remains in the saved example. Saturday remains Saturday. Nobody at the bakery has heard from us.
